claims.text: The starting phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloy typically forms an amorphous or near-amorphous structure under rapid quenching.
The starting alloy has marginal thermal stability and a tendency to crystallize.
Adding approximately 1–3 wt% boron will improve glass-forming ability relative to the boron-free alloy.
Adding approximately 1–3 wt% boron will enhance the thermal stability of the amorphous state relative to the boron-free alloy.
Boron addition produces local boron–phosphorus bonding configurations.
Local boron–phosphorus bonding configurations disrupt uniform nucleation of crystalline phases.
Boron atoms preferentially interact with phosphorus atoms in the alloy.
Boron–phosphorus interactions modify the local bonding network and increase atomic packing disorder.
The boron-induced local structure raises the energy barrier for crystallite nucleation during thermal activation.
The boron-modified alloy will have a higher crystallization onset temperature than the boron-free baseline.
The boron-modified alloy will have a broader supercooled liquid region than the boron-free baseline.
The boron-modified alloy will require a lower critical cooling rate for glass formation than the boron-free baseline.
The beneficial effect requires rapid-quenching conditions and a composition that supports significant boron–phosphorus interactions.
Boron concentrations below the optimal window may produce negligible changes.
Excessive boron additions may cause phase separation or unwanted crystalline phases.
Similar alloy systems have shown behavior analogous to the proposed boron effect.
